Current is signed charge flow per time: I=dQdtI = \frac{dQ}{dt}I=dtdQ​, or QΔt\frac{Q}{\Delta t}ΔtQ​ for a constant average flow. One ampere is one Cs\frac{C}{s}sC​. Conventional current points as positive charge would move. Electron drift in a metal points the opposite way. Random microscopic motion alone gives no net current. Current through a branch is a signed scalar; current density J is a vector.

Derive drift current and macroscopic resistance

In time Δt\Delta tΔt, carriers drift through volume AvdΔtAv_{d} \Delta tAvd​Δt. With number density n and charge magnitude |q|, charge crossing the area is nAvdΔt∣q∣nAv_{d} \Delta t \left| q \right|nAvd​Δt∣q∣. Divide by Δt\Delta tΔt:

I=n∣q∣Avd,J=I/A=n∣q∣vd,J=nqvd.I=n|q|Av_d,\quad J=I/A=n|q|v_d,\quad \mathbf J=nq\mathbf v_d.I=n∣q∣Avd​,J=I/A=n∣q∣vd​,J=nqvd​.

The vector expression keeps the signed charge. Carrier concentration has units m−3m^{-3}m−3, not Cm3\frac{C}{m^{3}}m3C​. Current from several carrier populations adds. J parallel to E is the simple isotropic ohmic model; it is not a universal statement for every medium and magnetic-field condition.

A 0.010 A0.010\,\mathrm{A}0.010A calculator for 60 s60\,\mathrm{s}60s transfers 0.600 C0.600\,\mathrm{C}0.600C. J=50 Am2J = 50\,\frac{\mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{m}^{2}}J=50m2A​, q=−0.10 Cq = - 0.10\,\mathrm{C}q=−0.10C, and vd=−2.0×10−4 msv_{d} = - 2.0 \times 10^{-4}\,\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}vd​=−2.0×10−4sm​ give n=J(qvd)=2.5×106 m−3n = \frac{J}{\left( qv_{d} \right)} = 2.5 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}n=(qvd​)J​=2.5×106m−3. The unusually large individual charge is the source's hypothetical value, not an electron charge.

For an ohmic isotropic material, E=ρJE = \rho JE=ρJ and conductivity σ=1ρ\sigma = \frac{1}{\rho}σ=ρ1​. Substitute E=VLE = \frac{V}{L}E=LV​ and J=IAJ = \frac{I}{A}J=AI​ for a uniform wire:

VL=ρIA⇒V=IR,R=ρLA,ρ=RAL.\frac VL=\rho\frac IA\Rightarrow V=IR,\quad R=\frac{\rho L}{A},\quad \rho=\frac{RA}{L}.LV​=ρAI​⇒V=IR,R=AρL​,ρ=LRA​.

Resistivity ρ\rhoρ has units Ω·m; resistance R has units Ω. For a circular wire A=πr2=πd24A = \pi r^{2} = \frac{\pi d^{2}}{4}A=πr2=4πd2​. Doubling LENGTH at fixed area doubles R. Doubling DIAMETER at fixed length divides R by four. For the same wire stretched without volume change, A=VwireLA = \frac{V_{\mathrm{wire}}}{L}A=LVwire​​, so R=ρL2VwireR = \frac{\rho L^{2}}{V_{\mathrm{wire}}}R=Vwire​ρL2​ if resistivity stays constant.

Temperature, ohmic behavior, and resistor identification

Near a reference temperature, R=R0[1+α(T−T0)]R = R_{0} \left[ 1 + \alpha \left( T - T_{0} \right) \right]R=R0​[1+α(T−T0​)], and similarly for resistivity. Rearrange α=(RR0−1)(T−T0)\alpha = \frac{\left( \frac{R}{R_{0}} - 1 \right)}{\left( T - T_{0} \right)}α=(T−T0​)(R0​R​−1)​. This linear approximation can fail over a large temperature range. Do not confuse the resistance-temperature coefficient with thermal-expansion α\alphaα. R0R_{0}R0​ is resistance when used in the R equation, despite the source's occasional “resistivity” label.

Ohm's law means a linear V–I relation under stable material conditions. A lamp heating up need not have a constant resistance. Carbon/semiconductor temperature behavior can differ from metals.

The source includes resistor color bands. For a four-band resistor, the first two colors give digits, the third gives a power-of-ten multiplier, and the fourth gives tolerance. Digit sequence: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, white 9. Gold/silver commonly represent multipliers 10−110−2\frac{10^{-1}}{10^{-2}}10−210−1​ or tolerances ±5%/±10%. Read the band roles and orientation, not only the colors.

Electrical power, energy, and internal resistance

An amount dq crossing voltage V transfers energy dW=VdqdW = VdqdW=Vdq. Divide by dt:

P=VI,PR=I2R=VR2/R,Eenergy=Pt.P=VI,\quad P_R=I^2R=V_R^2/R,\quad E_{energy}=Pt.P=VI,PR​=I2R=VR2​/R,Eenergy​=Pt.

The resistor substitutions require Ohm's law. A kilowatt-hour is an ENERGY unit: 1 kWh=3.6×106 J1\,\mathrm{kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{J}1kWh=3.6×106J. It is not “kilowatts per hour.” At fixed V, increasing R lowers resistor power; at fixed I, increasing R raises it.

A real source has emf E\mathcal{E}E and internal resistance r. For discharging current I, terminal voltage V=E−IrV = \mathcal{E} - IrV=E−Ir and I=E(R+r)I = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{\left( R + r \right)}I=(R+r)E​. During charging with current driven into the positive terminal, V=E+IrV = \mathcal{E} + IrV=E+Ir under that stated convention. Emf is energy supplied per charge, not a mechanical force.

Worked example — companion heating element. R=20ΩR = 20 \OmegaR=20Ω on 120 V120\,\mathrm{V}120V gives I=6 AI = 6\,\mathrm{A}I=6A and P=720 WP = 720\,\mathrm{W}P=720W. In 15 min=900 s15\,\mathrm{min} = 900\,\mathrm{s}15min=900s, energy: 648,000 J=0.18 kWh648{,}000\,\mathrm{J} = 0.18\,\mathrm{kWh}648,000J=0.18kWh. Increasing R to 30 Ω30\,\Omega30Ω at the same voltage gives 480 W480\,\mathrm{W}480W, not greater power.

Derive series and parallel resistor rules

Series resistors have a common current if there is no branch at their connecting node. Vtot=∑IRiV_{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum IR_{i}Vtot​=∑IRi​ gives Req=∑RiR_{\mathrm{eq}} = \sum R_{i}Req​=∑Ri​. Therefore ViVtot=RiReq\frac{V_{i}}{V_{\mathrm{tot}}} = \frac{R_{i}}{R_{\mathrm{eq}}}Vtot​Vi​​=Req​Ri​​: the voltage-divider relation.

Parallel resistors share the same two nodes and voltage. Itot=∑iVRiI_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_i\frac{V}{R_i}Itot​=∑i​Ri​V​ gives 1Req=∑i1Ri\frac1{R_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\sum_i\frac1{R_i}Req​1​=∑i​Ri​1​. For two, Req=R1R2(R1+R2)R_{\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{R_{1} R_{2}}{\left( R_{1} + R_{2} \right)}Req​=(R1​+R2​)R1​R2​​. Their current ratio is I1I2=R2R1\frac{I_{1}}{I_{2}} = \frac{R_{2}}{R_{1}}I2​I1​​=R1​R2​​. An equivalent parallel resistance must be smaller than the smallest positive branch resistance.

Worked example. Put 3 Ω3\,\Omega3Ω and 6 Ω6\,\Omega6Ω in parallel across 12 V12\,\mathrm{V}12V. Req=2ΩR_{\mathrm{eq}} = 2 \OmegaReq​=2Ω; branch currents are 4 A4\,\mathrm{A}4A and 2 A2\,\mathrm{A}2A; total is 6 A6\,\mathrm{A}6A. Total power: 12×6=72 W12 \times 6 = 72\,\mathrm{W}12×6=72W, also 42×3+22×6=72 W4^{2} \times 3 + 2^{2} \times 6 = 72\,\mathrm{W}42×3+22×6=72W. A series 4 Ω4\,\Omega4Ω added before that group gives 6 Ω6\,\Omega6Ω overall. The source current becomes 2 A2\,\mathrm{A}2A, the parallel-group drop becomes 4 V4\,\mathrm{V}4V, and its branch currents become 43A\frac{4}{3} A34​A and 23A\frac{2}{3} A32​A.

An ideal ammeter goes in SERIES and has zero resistance. An ideal voltmeter goes in PARALLEL and has infinite resistance. An ideal wire shorts points into one node. A shorted resistor has zero voltage, not its previous unmodified branch voltage. Do not reduce an arbitrary bridge as series/parallel when the required node conditions fail.

Kirchhoff rules: derive the equations and keep the signs

KCL follows conservation of charge at a steady node: ∑Iin=∑Iout\sum I_{\mathrm{in}} = \sum I_{\mathrm{out}}∑Iin​=∑Iout​. KVL follows energy balance around a lumped DC loop: ∑ΔV=0\sum \Delta V = 0∑ΔV=0. A resistor traversed with the chosen current gives −IR; traversed against it gives +IR. Across an ideal battery, negative-to-positive gives +E+ \mathcal{E}+E and the reverse gives −E- \mathcal{E}−E.

Choose arbitrary current directions, write independent equations, and solve them simultaneously. A negative answer reverses the assumed direction; it is not a negative physical resistance. Do not change an assumed arrow midway through the algebra.

Worked example — companion p. 14 type. A loop has a 12 V12\,\mathrm{V}12V aiding source, an opposing 6 V6\,\mathrm{V}6V source, and 6 Ω total resistance. KVL gives 12−6−6I=012 - 6 - 6 I = 012−6−6I=0, so I=1 AI = 1\,\mathrm{A}I=1A. If both sources aided, the same resistance would give 3 A3\,\mathrm{A}3A.

Transient energy extension. During a complete ideal RC charge from zero, the battery supplies ∫EIdt=CE2\int \mathcal{E} I dt = C\mathcal{E}^{2}∫EIdt=CE2. The capacitor stores CE22\frac{C\mathcal{E}^{2}}{2}2CE2​. The resistor dissipates the remaining CE22\frac{C\mathcal{E}^{2}}{2}2CE2​, independent of positive R in this model. A smaller R changes the time and peak power; it does not remove that total dissipated energy.

Source problems · full working

Finish the current, resistivity, and resistor-identification material

Current carriers. The primary's “flow of electrons” definition describes a metal, but current more generally means net charge flow. Positive and negative ions can also carry current. A closed circuit provides a continuous conducting path. An open branch carries no steady conduction current in this model. A short circuit provides a low-resistance path; an actual source's internal resistance still limits its current.

Circuit symbols — primary p. 37. The longer battery line marks the positive terminal. An A in a circle denotes an ammeter in the measured branch. A V in a circle denotes a voltmeter connected across two nodes. A connection dot identifies joined wires. Label the nodes before deciding whether two components share a voltage.

Current and the body — primary p. 15. The source table associates increasing current with sensation, muscle effects, disrupted breathing, and heart effects. Its ranges are illustrative, not universal thresholds. Effects also depend on the current path and contact duration. OSHA's electrical-safety material explains these dependencies. The original table remains available in the source reader.

Drift, collision time, and microscopic Ohm's law

Source starting point: Primary p. 7. The additional algebra uses a simple relaxation-time model.

  1. Between collisions, the carrier acceleration is a=qEma = \frac{qE}{m}a=mqE​.
  2. The model's mean drift velocity is vd=qEτcollisionmv_{d} = \frac{qE\tau _{\mathrm{collision}}}{m}vd​=mqEτcollision​​.
  3. Insert vd into J=nqvdJ = nqv_{d}J=nqvd​.
  4. Compare the result with J=σEJ = \sigma EJ=σE.
J=nq2τcollisionmE,σ=nq2τcollisionm,ρ=mnq2τcollision.\begin{gathered}\mathbf J=\frac{nq^2\tau_{collision}}m\mathbf E, \\\sigma=\frac{nq^2\tau_{collision}}m, \\\rho=\frac{m}{nq^2\tau_{collision}}.\end{gathered}J=mnq2τcollision​​E,σ=mnq2τcollision​​,ρ=nq2τcollision​m​.​

The squared charge makes σ\sigmaσ positive for either carrier sign. For electrons, vd opposes E while J points along E. This is a microscopic model for suitable materials; it is not an exact conductivity theory for every substance.

The companion also lists conductors, semiconductors, and insulators. Metals generally have low resistivity. Insulators have much higher resistivity. Semiconductor resistivity strongly depends on temperature and impurities. Its graph shows that superconducting resistivity becomes zero below a material-dependent critical temperature under suitable conditions. Do not extrapolate the room-temperature linear resistance model through that transition.

Four, five, and six bands. Four bands use two significant digits, a multiplier, and tolerance. Five bands use three significant digits, a multiplier, and tolerance. Six bands add a temperature coefficient, commonly expressed in parts per million per kelvin. The source's pictured six-band resistor is green–blue–black–red–gold–yellow.

Source correction — primary p. 66. Different independent loops do not have to use the same traversal direction. Each loop can use either direction. Keep the signs consistent within that traversal. Reversing one complete loop equation multiplies it by −1 without changing the physical solution.

RC circuits: complete logarithms, limits, and switching checks

Derivation∴

Discharge from the differential equation to the time formula

Sources: Primary pp. 77–79. Let q be the charge remaining on the initially positive plate. The discharge-current magnitude is −dqdt- \frac{dq}{dt}−dtdq​.

  1. Use the loop equation R(dqdt)+qC=0R \left( \frac{dq}{dt} \right) + \frac{q}{C} = 0R(dtdq​)+Cq​=0 under this charge convention.
  2. Separate variables: dqq=−dt(RC)\frac{dq}{q} = - \frac{dt}{\left( RC \right)}qdq​=−(RC)dt​.
  3. Integrate from Q0Q_{0}Q0​ to q(t) and from 0 to t.
  4. Exponentiate, divide by C for voltage, then isolate time when needed.
ln⁡qQ0=−tRC⇒q=Q0e−t/RC,VC=V0e−t/RC,t=RCln⁡V0VC.\ln\frac{q}{Q_0}=-\frac{t}{RC} \Rightarrow q=Q_0e^{-t/RC}, \qquad V_C=V_0e^{-t/RC}, \qquad t=RC\ln\frac{V_0}{V_C}.lnQ0​q​=−RCt​⇒q=Q0​e−t/RC,VC​=V0​e−t/RC,t=RClnVC​V0​​.

The logarithm uses a dimensionless ratio. For a decay fraction f=VCV0f = \frac{V_{C}}{V_{0}}f=V0​VC​​, use 0<f≤10 < f \le 10<f≤1. Reaching exactly zero takes infinite time in the ideal exponential model.

The source's 35 μF35\,\mathrm{\mu F}35μF, 120 Ω discharge problem

Initial and final conditions. An initially uncharged capacitor has VC(0)=0V_{C} \left( 0 \right) = 0VC​(0)=0 and initially behaves as a zero-voltage element in the charging circuit. At DC steady state, its current tends to zero. A precharged capacitor is not initially a zero-voltage element. Use VC(t)=Vf+(Vinitial−Vf)exp⁡(−tτ)V_{C} \left( t \right) = V_{f} + \left( V_{\mathrm{initial}} - V_{f} \right) \exp \left( - \frac{t}{\tau} \right)VC​(t)=Vf​+(Vinitial​−Vf​)exp(−τt​) when the initial voltage is nonzero.

Timing applications. Wipers, traffic-light timers, camera flashes, and pacemaker timing circuits use charging or discharging intervals. The elementary RC model explains a time scale; it does not represent every control function inside those devices.

Situational problems: choose the law, then solve

These added practice problems apply the module concepts. They are not copied examination questions. Keep the stated assumptions when you use each result.

Situation 1: Stretching a wire

A uniform wire is stretched to twice its length. Its volume and resistivity remain constant. The same ideal voltage is applied before and after stretching. How does the current change?

  1. Conserve volume.
Af(2L)=AiL ⇒ Af=Ai/2A_f(2L)=A_iL\ \Rightarrow\ A_f=A_i/2Af​(2L)=Ai​L ⇒ Af​=Ai​/2
  1. Compare resistances.
Rf=ρ2LAi/2=4RiR_f=\rho\frac{2L}{A_i/2}=4R_iRf​=ρAi​/22L​=4Ri​
  1. Use fixed voltage.
If=V/Rf=Ii/4I_f=V/R_f=I_i/4If​=V/Rf​=Ii​/4
  1. Check the assumption. The result assumes that temperature and resistivity do not change.

Answer: It becomes one quarter of its original value.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • It becomes one half. — This ignores the reduction in cross-sectional area.
  • It stays constant. — The resistance changes even though the material volume stays constant.
  • It doubles. — At fixed voltage, increasing resistance decreases current.

Situation 2: Loaded battery voltage

A battery has fixed emf and positive internal resistance. Its external load resistance increases. Use the steady DC model. What happens to its delivered current and terminal voltage?

  1. Write the loop current.
I=E/(R+r)I=\mathcal E/(R+r)I=E/(R+r)
  1. Relate terminal voltage to internal drop.
Vterm=E−IrV_{\mathrm{term}}=\mathcal E-IrVterm​=E−Ir

  1. Increase the load resistance. The denominator increases, so current and internal drop decrease.

  2. Check the open-circuit limit. As load resistance approaches infinity, current approaches zero and terminal voltage approaches the emf.

Answer: Current decreases; terminal voltage increases toward the emf.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • Both decrease. — The internal voltage drop decreases as current decreases.
  • Current increases; terminal voltage decreases. — Increasing total series resistance decreases the current.
  • Both remain constant. — Internal resistance makes terminal voltage depend on load current.

Situation 3: A capacitor at a switching instant

An ideal capacitor initially has a nonzero voltage. A switch connects it through a finite resistor to a different constant voltage source. Which statement applies immediately after switching?

  1. Start from the capacitor relation.
i=C dVC/dti=C\,dV_C/dti=CdVC​/dt

  1. Apply finite-current behavior. Finite current changes the charge continuously.

  2. Apply the loop equation at the instant.

i(0+)=Vs−VC(0−)Ri(0^+)=\frac{V_s-V_C(0^-)}{R}i(0+)=RVs​−VC​(0−)​
  1. Separate the two quantities. Continuity of capacitor voltage does not require continuity of resistor current.

Answer: Capacitor voltage stays continuous; resistor current can change immediately.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • Capacitor voltage instantly equals the source voltage. — The finite resistor limits current and prevents an instantaneous change in stored charge.
  • Capacitor current must be zero because the initial voltage is fixed. — The voltage is continuous at the instant, but its time derivative can be nonzero.
  • Capacitor voltage and resistor current must both be continuous. — The resistor has no energy-storage requirement that forces current continuity.

Situation 4: A negative Kirchhoff result

You choose clockwise current for one branch and solve consistent Kirchhoff equations. The branch current is negative. What does that result mean?

  1. Keep the original arrows. Use the same current arrows throughout the equations.

  2. Read the solved sign. A negative value reverses the physical direction relative to its reference arrow.

  3. Check resistor power.

PR=I2R≥0(R>0)P_R=I^2R\ge0\quad(R>0)PR​=I2R≥0(R>0)
  1. Verify the equations. Substitute the signed result into the original node and loop equations.

Answer: The actual current flows opposite to the chosen arrow.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • The circuit violates charge conservation. — A negative signed current can satisfy charge conservation.
  • The resistor has negative resistance. — A negative current alone does not imply negative resistance.
  • Replace the current with its magnitude in every equation without changing signs. — The signed solution must remain consistent with the original reference directions.

Situation 5: Removing one parallel branch

Two resistors connect in parallel across an ideal constant-voltage source. One branch is removed. What happens to current in the remaining resistor and total source current?

  1. Use the maintained voltage.
Iremaining=V/RI_{\mathrm{remaining}}=V/RIremaining​=V/R
  1. Add the original branch currents.
Itotal,i=V/R1+V/R2I_{\mathrm{total,i}}=V/R_1+V/R_2Itotal,i​=V/R1​+V/R2​
  1. Remove the disconnected branch.
Itotal,f=V/R1I_{\mathrm{total,f}}=V/R_1Itotal,f​=V/R1​
  1. Check the source assumption. A real battery with internal resistance can also change its terminal voltage.

Answer: Remaining-branch current stays the same; total current decreases.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • Both currents increase. — Removing a parallel path increases equivalent resistance.
  • Remaining-branch current doubles because it receives the removed current. — An ideal voltage source does not maintain fixed total current.
  • Both become zero. — The remaining branch still forms a closed circuit.

Situation 6: Load power with internal resistance

A 12 V battery with 1.0 Ω internal resistance supplies a 5.0 Ω load. Find the steady power delivered to the load.

  1. Include both series resistances.
Rtotal=5+1=6 ΩR_{\mathrm{total}}=5+1=6\,\OmegaRtotal​=5+1=6Ω
  1. Find the current.
I=12/6=2 AI=12/6=2\,\mathrm AI=12/6=2A
  1. Find the load voltage.
VL=IRL=2(5)=10 VV_L=IR_L=2(5)=10\,\mathrm VVL​=IRL​=2(5)=10V
  1. Calculate only the load power.
PL=I2RL=22(5)=20 WP_L=I^2R_L=2^2(5)=20\,\mathrm WPL​=I2RL​=22(5)=20W
  1. Check energy per second.
EI=24 W=PL+I2r=20+4\mathcal EI=24\,\mathrm W=P_L+I^2r=20+4EI=24W=PL​+I2r=20+4
  1. State the result.
20 W20\,\mathrm W20W

Answer: 20 W20\,\mathrm W20W

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 24 W24\,\mathrm W24W — This is total source power, including internal heating.
  • 28.8 W28.8\,\mathrm W28.8W — This treats the full emf as the load voltage.
  • 4 W4\,\mathrm W4W — This is power dissipated in the internal resistance.

Situation 7: Stretching changes wire power

A uniform 3.0 Ω wire is stretched to twice its length at constant volume and resistivity. It is then connected across an ideal 12 V source. Find its new electrical power.

  1. Conserve material volume.
Af=Ai/2A_f=A_i/2Af​=Ai​/2
  1. Use both geometric changes.
Rf=ρ2LAi/2=4(3)=12 ΩR_f=\rho\frac{2L}{A_i/2}=4(3)=12\,\OmegaRf​=ρAi​/22L​=4(3)=12Ω
  1. Use fixed-voltage power.
Pf=V2/Rf=122/12=12 WP_f=V^2/R_f=12^2/12=12\,\mathrm WPf​=V2/Rf​=122/12=12W

  1. Check the trend. The larger resistance reduces power at fixed voltage. Fixed-current operation would give a different trend.

  2. State the result.

12 W12\,\mathrm W12W

Situation 8: Find a charging time from voltage

An initially uncharged 100 μF capacitor charges through 2.0 kΩ from an ideal 9.0 V source. Find the time when capacitor voltage first reaches 6.0 V.

  1. Convert and calculate the time constant.
τ=RC=(2000)(100×10−6)=0.200 s\tau=RC=(2000)(100\times10^{-6})=0.200\,\mathrm sτ=RC=(2000)(100×10−6)=0.200s
  1. Choose charging from zero.
VC=Vs(1−e−t/τ)V_C=V_s(1-e^{-t/\tau})VC​=Vs​(1−e−t/τ)
  1. Isolate the exponential.
e−t/τ=1−6/9=1/3e^{-t/\tau}=1-6/9=1/3e−t/τ=1−6/9=1/3
  1. Take logarithms.
t=−τln⁡(1/3)=0.200ln⁡3t=-\tau\ln(1/3)=0.200\ln3t=−τln(1/3)=0.200ln3
  1. Check the current at this instant.
I=(9−6)/2000=1.50 mAI=(9-6)/2000=1.50\,\mathrm{mA}I=(9−6)/2000=1.50mA
  1. State the result.
0.219722 s0.219722\,\mathrm s0.219722s

Answer: 0.219722 s0.219722\,\mathrm s0.219722s

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 0.2 s0.2\,\mathrm s0.2s — One time constant gives about 63.2% of the final voltage, not 6/9.
  • 0.081093 s0.081093\,\mathrm s0.081093s — This uses the wrong logarithm argument.
  • 0.6 s0.6\,\mathrm s0.6s — The voltage does not rise linearly with time.

Vp=IRp=4 VV_p=IR_p=4\,\mathrm VVp​=IRp​=4V

P3=Vp2/3=16/3 WP_3=V_p^2/3=16/3\,\mathrm WP3​=Vp2​/3=16/3W
  1. Check branch currents.
I3=4/3 A,I6=4/6 A,I3+I6=2 AI_3=4/3\,\mathrm A,\quad I_6=4/6\,\mathrm A,\quad I_3+I_6=2\,\mathrm AI3​=4/3A,I6​=4/6A,I3​+I6​=2A

Situation 10: A source receives current

Three branches connect the same upper node to ground. Branch 1 has a 12 V ideal source in series with 3 Ω. Branch 2 has a 3 V ideal source in series with 6 Ω. Both source positive terminals point toward the upper node. Branch 3 is a 2 Ω load. Find the signed current delivered by the 3 V source toward the upper node.

  1. Define the reference. Let V be upper-node voltage. Positive source current flows toward that node.

  2. Apply node conservation.

12−V3+3−V6=V2\frac{12-V}{3}+\frac{3-V}{6}=\frac V2312−V​+63−V​=2V​
  1. Solve the node voltage.
2(12−V)+(3−V)=3V ⇒ V=4.5 V2(12-V)+(3-V)=3V\ \Rightarrow\ V=4.5\,\mathrm V2(12−V)+(3−V)=3V ⇒ V=4.5V
  1. Calculate the requested signed branch current.
I2=(3−4.5)/6=−0.250 AI_2=(3-4.5)/6=-0.250\,\mathrm AI2​=(3−4.5)/6=−0.250A

  1. Interpret the sign. Current enters the positive terminal of the 3 V source. The ideal source absorbs electrical energy in this model.

  2. State the result.

−0.25 A-0.25\,\mathrm A−0.25A

Answer: −0.25 A-0.25\,\mathrm A−0.25A

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 0.25 A0.25\,\mathrm A0.25A — This removes the sign that identifies current entering the source.
  • 0.5 A0.5\,\mathrm A0.5A — This ignores the shared node voltage and the other source.
  • 1.5 A1.5\,\mathrm A1.5A — This is the current delivered by the 12 V branch, not the requested branch.

Situation 15: A voltage divider with a load · model check

An ideal 12 V source supplies a divider with upper resistor R1=100 ΩR_1=100\,\OmegaR1​=100Ω and lower resistor R2=200 ΩR_2=200\,\OmegaR2​=200Ω. A load RL=300 ΩR_L=300\,\OmegaRL​=300Ω connects across R2. Use steady DC conditions and ideal wires. Why does connecting the load change the output voltage of this divider?

  1. Identify what stays fixed. The load is parallel to the lower resistor. Calculate the loaded equivalent resistance before applying the voltage-divider relation.

  2. Reduce the loaded lower branch.

Rp=R2RL/(R2+RL)=120 ΩR_p=R_2R_L/(R_2+R_L)=120\,\OmegaRp​=R2​RL​/(R2​+RL​)=120Ω
  1. Find source current and load voltage.
I=V/(R1+Rp)=0.0545455 A,VL=IRp=6.54545 VI=V/(R_1+R_p)=0.0545455\,\mathrm A,\quad V_L=IR_p=6.54545\,\mathrm VI=V/(R1​+Rp​)=0.0545455A,VL​=IRp​=6.54545V
  1. Apply the conclusion. The source voltage is fixed, but its division between the two series branches changes.

Answer: The load changes the equivalent resistance of the lower branch.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • An ideal source must reduce its specified voltage whenever current rises. — That behavior belongs to a source with internal resistance.
  • The upper resistor automatically changes resistance. — Its specified resistance stays fixed.
  • Parallel components always have equal current. — They have equal voltage; their currents depend on resistance.

Situation 25: A warm resistor on a real battery · model check

A wire has resistance 6 Ω at 20°C and linear temperature coefficient 0.0040 K−10.0040\,\mathrm{K^{-1}}0.0040K−1. Why must the problem specify that the wire temperature is held fixed?

  1. Identify what stays fixed. First update the wire resistance using the temperature difference. Then include internal resistance in the complete circuit.

  2. Find the wire resistance at the stated temperature.

R=R0[1+α(T−T0)]=7.2 ΩR=R_0[1+\alpha(T-T_0)]=7.2\,\OmegaR=R0​[1+α(T−T0​)]=7.2Ω

  1. Find terminal voltage.
Vt=E−Ir=10.5366 VV_t=\mathcal E-Ir=10.5366\,\mathrm VVt​=E−Ir=10.5366V
  1. Apply the conclusion. The stated circuit calculation uses the specified operating temperature.

Answer: Otherwise electrical heating can change resistance and current until a thermal balance is reached.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • Ohm’s law cannot be used at any temperature other than 20°C. — Use the resistance appropriate to the stated temperature.

Situation 52: Maximum power from a resistive source · Find the maximum delivered load power

A battery has fixed emf 12 V and fixed internal resistance 2 Ω. A variable positive load resistance R connects to it. Assume steady DC behavior. Find the operating point that maximizes power delivered to the load, rather than total source power or efficiency. Find the maximum delivered load power.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. Load power depends on both load resistance and the current it allows. Differentiate the full expression rather than treating current as fixed.

  2. Write load power as a function of the adjustable load.

PL(R)=(ER+r)2RP_L(R)=\left(\frac{\mathcal E}{R+r}\right)^2RPL​(R)=(R+rE​)2R
  1. Differentiate and use the positive-resistance domain.
dPLdR=E2(r−R)(R+r)3=0 ⇒ R=r\frac{dP_L}{dR}=\frac{\mathcal E^2(r-R)}{(R+r)^3}=0\ \Rightarrow\ R=rdRdPL​​=(R+r)3E2(r−R)​=0 ⇒ R=r
  1. Check the two limiting cases.
PL→0 as R→0 or R→∞P_L\to0\text{ as }R\to0\text{ or }R\to\inftyPL​→0 as R→0 or R→∞
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
PL,max⁡=E2/(4r)=122/(4(2))P_{L,\max}=\mathcal E^2/(4r)=12^2/(4(2))PL,max​=E2/(4r)=122/(4(2))

  1. Check the physical result. At the optimum, equal internal and load resistances dissipate equal powers.

  2. State the result.

18 W18\,\mathrm W18W

Answer: 18 W18\,\mathrm W18W

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 72 W72\,\mathrm W72W — This uses the short-circuit current while also assigning full emf to the load.
  • 36 W36\,\mathrm W36W — This is total source power at the maximum-load-power point.
  • 9 W9\,\mathrm W9W — This adds an extra factor of two not present in the power relation.

Situation 53: Maximum power from a resistive source · Find the current at the maximum-load-power point

A battery has fixed emf 12 V and fixed internal resistance 2 Ω. A variable positive load resistance R connects to it. Assume steady DC behavior. Find the operating point that maximizes power delivered to the load, rather than total source power or efficiency. Find the current at the maximum-load-power point.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. Load power depends on both load resistance and the current it allows. Differentiate the full expression rather than treating current as fixed.

  2. Write load power as a function of the adjustable load.

PL(R)=(ER+r)2RP_L(R)=\left(\frac{\mathcal E}{R+r}\right)^2RPL​(R)=(R+rE​)2R
  1. Differentiate and use the positive-resistance domain.
dPLdR=E2(r−R)(R+r)3=0 ⇒ R=r\frac{dP_L}{dR}=\frac{\mathcal E^2(r-R)}{(R+r)^3}=0\ \Rightarrow\ R=rdRdPL​​=(R+r)3E2(r−R)​=0 ⇒ R=r
  1. Check the two limiting cases.
PL→0 as R→0 or R→∞P_L\to0\text{ as }R\to0\text{ or }R\to\inftyPL​→0 as R→0 or R→∞
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
Iopt=E/(2r)=12/(2(2))I_{\rm opt}=\mathcal E/(2r)=12/(2(2))Iopt​=E/(2r)=12/(2(2))

  1. Check the physical result. The optimum current is half the idealized short-circuit current.

  2. State the result.

3 A3\,\mathrm A3A

Answer: 3 A3\,\mathrm A3A

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 6 A6\,\mathrm A6A — This is short-circuit current.
  • 1.5 A1.5\,\mathrm A1.5A — The total resistance at the optimum is 2r, not 4r.
  • 0 A0\,\mathrm A0A — An open circuit delivers no load power.

Situation 54: Maximum power from a resistive source · Find the loaded terminal voltage at maximum load power

A battery has fixed emf 12 V and fixed internal resistance 2 Ω. A variable positive load resistance R connects to it. Assume steady DC behavior. Find the operating point that maximizes power delivered to the load, rather than total source power or efficiency. Find the loaded terminal voltage at maximum load power.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. Load power depends on both load resistance and the current it allows. Differentiate the full expression rather than treating current as fixed.

  2. Write load power as a function of the adjustable load.

PL(R)=(ER+r)2RP_L(R)=\left(\frac{\mathcal E}{R+r}\right)^2RPL​(R)=(R+rE​)2R
  1. Differentiate and use the positive-resistance domain.
dPLdR=E2(r−R)(R+r)3=0 ⇒ R=r\frac{dP_L}{dR}=\frac{\mathcal E^2(r-R)}{(R+r)^3}=0\ \Rightarrow\ R=rdRdPL​​=(R+r)3E2(r−R)​=0 ⇒ R=r
  1. Check the two limiting cases.
PL→0 as R→0 or R→∞P_L\to0\text{ as }R\to0\text{ or }R\to\inftyPL​→0 as R→0 or R→∞
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
Vt=E−Ir=E/2=6 VV_t=\mathcal E-Ir=\mathcal E/2=6\,\mathrm VVt​=E−Ir=E/2=6V

  1. Check the physical result. Maximum delivered load power does not mean maximum electrical efficiency.

  2. State the result.

6 V6\,\mathrm V6V

Answer: 6 V6\,\mathrm V6V

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 12 V12\,\mathrm V12V — Half the emf is lost across the internal resistance at this operating point.
  • 0 V0\,\mathrm V0V — This describes a short circuit, not the maximum-power load.
  • 3 V3\,\mathrm V3V — The load and internal voltage drops are equal, not in a one-to-three ratio.

Situation 55: Maximum power from a resistive source · model check

A battery has fixed emf 12 V and fixed internal resistance 2 Ω. A variable positive load resistance R connects to it. Assume steady DC behavior. Find the operating point that maximizes power delivered to the load, rather than total source power or efficiency. Why is maximum load power different from maximum efficiency in this source model?

  1. Identify what stays fixed. Load power depends on both load resistance and the current it allows. Differentiate the full expression rather than treating current as fixed.

  2. Write load power as a function of the adjustable load.

PL(R)=(ER+r)2RP_L(R)=\left(\frac{\mathcal E}{R+r}\right)^2RPL​(R)=(R+rE​)2R
  1. Differentiate and use the positive-resistance domain.
dPLdR=E2(r−R)(R+r)3=0 ⇒ R=r\frac{dP_L}{dR}=\frac{\mathcal E^2(r-R)}{(R+r)^3}=0\ \Rightarrow\ R=rdRdPL​​=(R+r)3E2(r−R)​=0 ⇒ R=r
  1. Check the two limiting cases.
PL→0 as R→0 or R→∞P_L\to0\text{ as }R\to0\text{ or }R\to\inftyPL​→0 as R→0 or R→∞
  1. Apply the conclusion. Efficiency approaches one only at very small current, where delivered load power approaches zero.

Answer: At maximum load power, half the source power heats the internal resistance.

Why the other answers do not work:

  • Internal resistance dissipates no power at the optimum. — Its current equals the load current and its resistance equals the optimum load resistance.
  • An open circuit delivers the largest load power. — Its current is zero, so delivered power is zero.
  • A short circuit delivers the largest load voltage. — Its external load voltage is zero in this model.

Situation 56: Maximum power from a resistive source · Find the load resistance for maximum delivered load power

A battery has fixed emf 18 V and fixed internal resistance 3 Ω. A variable positive load resistance R connects to it. Assume steady DC behavior. Find the operating point that maximizes power delivered to the load, rather than total source power or efficiency. Find the load resistance for maximum delivered load power.

  1. Identify the model and the conditions. Load power depends on both load resistance and the current it allows. Differentiate the full expression rather than treating current as fixed.

  2. Write load power as a function of the adjustable load.

PL(R)=(ER+r)2RP_L(R)=\left(\frac{\mathcal E}{R+r}\right)^2RPL​(R)=(R+rE​)2R
  1. Differentiate and use the positive-resistance domain.
dPLdR=E2(r−R)(R+r)3=0 ⇒ R=r\frac{dP_L}{dR}=\frac{\mathcal E^2(r-R)}{(R+r)^3}=0\ \Rightarrow\ R=rdRdPL​​=(R+r)3E2(r−R)​=0 ⇒ R=r
  1. Check the two limiting cases.
PL→0 as R→0 or R→∞P_L\to0\text{ as }R\to0\text{ or }R\to\inftyPL​→0 as R→0 or R→∞
  1. Solve the requested quantity.
Ropt=r=3 ΩR_{\rm opt}=r=3\,\OmegaRopt​=r=3Ω

  1. Check the physical result. The stationary point is a maximum because power falls to zero at both resistance limits.

  2. State the result.

3 Ω3\,\Omega3Ω

Answer: 3 Ω3\,\Omega3Ω

Why the other answers do not work:

  • 0 Ω0\,\Omega0Ω — A short circuit has zero load voltage and zero load power.
  • 6 Ω6\,\Omega6Ω — The derivative vanishes at R=rR=rR=r, not 2r.
  • 1.5 Ω1.5\,\Omega1.5Ω — This gives a smaller load than the maximum-power condition.
